ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure is an ideal operational amplifier circuit. The right side of the op-amp triangle is the output terminal, labeled uo; the lower one with “+” is the non-inverting input terminal, and the upper one with “-” is the inverting input terminal. The input signal ui is connected to the non-inverting input terminal through a 10 kΩ resistor, and this non-inverting input node is also connected to ground through a 10 kΩ resistor. The inverting input terminal is connected to ground through a 10 kΩ resistor, and at the same time is connected to the output uo through a 10 kΩ resistor at the top, forming negative feedback. Reasoning: The input current of an ideal op-amp is 0, so the non-inverting terminal voltage is obtained by voltage division of the two equal 10 kΩ resistors between ui and ground, V+ = ui·10k/(10k+10k) = ui/2. The inverting terminal voltage is obtained by voltage division of the two equal 10 kΩ resistors between output uo and ground, V− = uo·10k/(10k+10k) = uo/2. Under linear negative feedback, an ideal op-amp satisfies a virtual short, V− = V+, therefore uo/2 = ui/2, obtaining uo/ui = 1.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: identify the op-amp terminals, the output uo, the input ui, and the four 10 kΩ resistors. Compute the non-inverting input voltage as V+ = ui·10k/(10k+10k) = ui/2 because no op-amp input current flows. Compute the inverting input voltage from the feedback divider as V− = uo·10k/(10k+10k) = uo/2. Apply the ideal-op-amp virtual short V− = V+, giving uo/2 = ui/2, so the voltage gain uo/ui = 1.
